html:
A collection of Roman imperial laws issued from the reign of Constantine to 437, published by Theodosius II in 438. It took effect in both the eastern and western halves of the empire on 1 January 439, with the western emperor Valentinian III joining in.

A commission began work in 429. It gathered laws from archives and copies across the empire and sorted them by topic into 16 books, with more than 2,500 entries. The last book deals with religion: the status of the church, the clergy, heretics, Jews and pagans. It includes the Edict of Thessalonica.

It was the first official code of Roman law since the Twelve Tables. In the east it was replaced by Justinian's code in 529. In the west it lived on: in 506 the Visigothic king Alaric II issued a shortened version for his Roman subjects, the Breviary of Alaric, which kept much of it alive in medieval Europe.
